w: A 226-acre rural cemetery established in 1863, designed by Frederick Law Olmsted -- the landscape architect behind Central Park and Prospect Park. Many of California's historical figures are buried here, some along the ridge nicknamed Millionaires' Row for its Bay views. Docent tours have run since 1970.

Ridge section nicknamed Millionaires' Row for its Bay views
Docent tours have run since 1970

n: Cathedral of Saint Francis de Sales
w: Built in 1893, this church became the cathedral of the Roman Catholic Diocese of Oakland in 1962. It served in that role until the 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake damaged the building, ending its 27-year run as the diocese's seat.
_facts: Built in 1893
Cathedral of the Roman Catholic Diocese of Oakland from 1962
Damaged by the 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake

w: Oakland's waterfront district, named for the author and owned by the Port of Oakland. Landmarks include the historic Heinold's First and Last Chance Saloon and the relocated cabin where London once lived in the Klondike. The former presidential yacht USS Potomac moors at an adjacent slip.
s: Oakland's waterfront named for author Jack London

w: Founded in 1875 as the First Hebrew Congregation of Oakland, the oldest Jewish congregation in the East Bay. Early members studying at its Sabbath school included Gertrude Stein and Judah Leon Magnes. The 1914 Beaux-Arts sanctuary, designed by G. Albert Lansburgh, is the oldest synagogue building in Oakland.
_facts: Founded 1875 as the First Hebrew Congregation of Oakland
Gertrude Stein attended its Sabbath school as a child
1914 Beaux-Arts sanctuary by G. Albert Lansburgh is Oakland's oldest synagogue building

w: Franklin D. Roosevelt's presidential yacht from 1936 until his death in 1945. On 3 August 1941 it played a decoy role while Roosevelt held the secret conference that produced the Atlantic Charter. Now preserved in Oakland as a National Historic Landmark, it is the only former presidential yacht open to the public.
s: FDR's yacht, now the only one open to the public

w: A nonprofit at 355 24th Street providing studios, supplies and gallery space to artists with developmental, mental and physical disabilities. It is one of the oldest and largest art centers of its kind anywhere in the world.
